svg.text: 🧩 Creating Custom Skills
Agent Skills with Anthropic · DeepLearning.AI — how a skill is structured, and the best practices for production skills.
Essence: A skill is one folder holding a SKILL.md file — a YAML frontmatter (name + description) plus a
Markdown body of instructions — with optional scripts, references, and assets that load only when they are actually needed.
The name and description are mission-critical: they tell the agent what the skill does and when to trigger it.
🗂️ Skill structure — anatomy of a skill
One skill = one folder named exactly like the skill. Only SKILL.md is required; everything else is optional.
SKILL.md — the only required file
YAML frontmatter — name + description (required), plus optional metadata fields.
Markdown body — step-by-step instructions, input / output format, and common edge cases.
Optional directories — referenced from SKILL.md and loaded only when needed (progressive disclosure):
/scripts
Code to run; document its
dependencies + error handling.
/references
Extra docs read on demand;
add a table of contents if >100 lines.
/assets
Output templates, images,
logos, data files, schemas.
📇 Frontmatter — the required fields
name
• Maximum 64 characters; only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens (never start or end with a hyphen).
• Must match the parent folder name exactly, or the skill will not load.
• Recommended: use the gerund (verb + -ing) form, e.g. generating-practice-questions.
description
• Maximum 1024 characters, non-empty. Describe both what the skill does and when to use it.
• Lean into specific keywords that should make the agent trigger this skill.
Optional fields also exist: license, compatibility (max 500 chars), metadata (arbitrary key-value), allowed-tools (experimental).
📝 Body content — best practices
There are no format restrictions on the body, but for predictable workflows follow these habits:
• Give clear step-by-step instructions, an input / output format, and the common edge cases.
• Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines — move detailed material into separate reference files.
• Use progressive disclosure: show the basics, link to advanced / domain content loaded only when needed.
• Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md (avoid nested file references).
• Be clear and concise; use consistent terminology.
• Always use forward slashes in file paths — even on Windows — so the skill works across environments.
The agent-skills specification is still evolving, so some existing skills (even Anthropic's) do not yet follow it exactly.
🎚️ Degrees of freedom — how much to constrain the skill
High freedom — general text-based directions; many approaches are valid (good for creative output).
Medium freedom — instructions give customizable pseudocode or patterns; a preferred way, some variation OK.
Low freedom — instructions point to specific scripts; one exact sequence must be followed (best for best-practice tasks).
For complex work, break into small sequential skills rather than one huge skill — systems can handle 100+ skills.
🧪 Example 1 — generating-practice-questions
Goal: generate educational practice questions from lecture notes to test understanding. A medium-freedom skill.
• Input — supported formats: PDF (extract with pdfplumber), LaTeX, Markdown, plain text; pull out learning objectives.
• Question structure — a fixed order: True/False → Explanatory → Coding → Use Case, each with sub-guidelines.
• Output depends on the request; instead of inlining every example, it points to assets/ templates (LaTeX, Markdown).
• Domain-specific examples live in references/, loaded only when needed — efficient use of the context window.
Skill-creator score: 9/10 — mainly could tighten the input-format section for conciseness.
🧪 Example 2 — analyzing-time-series
Goal: understand a time-series CSV before forecasting. A low-freedom, deterministic workflow built on 3 Python scripts
(visualize.py, diagnose.py, ts_utils.py). The body pins the exact steps to run, in order:
Step 1 · Diagnose
run diagnose.py → summary.txt
Step 2 · Plots (optional)
run visualize.py → plots/
Step 3 · Report
summarize + interpret findings
• Guidance for reading results lives in references/interpretation.md; the output is a fixed tree of files and folders.
• Because scripts need libraries, the skill lists dependencies explicitly so they can be installed.
Dependencies: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels, scipy. · Skill-creator score: 10/10 (exemplary, only 79 lines).
🔎 Evaluate skills with the skill-creator
Run your finished skills through the skill-creator skill — it checks them against best practices out of the box.
• In Claude Code it is not built in, so install it from a marketplace: add anthropic/skills (holds two collections —
document-skills for Excel / PowerPoint / Word / PDF, and example-skills including skill-creator).
• Install at project scope, restart Claude Code (it writes enabledPlugins to .claude/settings.json), check with /skills.
• Ask it to evaluate your skills, using two subagents in parallel — one per skill — for a fast first review.
• It scores each criterion (frontmatter, conciseness, degrees of freedom, progressive disclosure, no duplication…)
and returns concrete recommendations you can act on before shipping.
Results here: generating-practice-questions 9/10, analyzing-time-series 10/10.
✅ Evaluation — write unit tests for skills
Best-practice checks are not enough — also test that the skill actually works, like a software unit test.
A test harness names the skills, a set of queries, the input files, and the expected_behavior. For example:
• practice-questions — query "generate and save to .md / .tex / .pdf"; expect correct library, objectives
extracted, all 4 question types, correct templates, LaTeX compiles, saved to the right file.
• time-series — assume the scripts are unit-tested; verify the workflow runs in the correct order, returns a
summary, interprets findings, and creates the results folder with every file in its right place.
Also: gather human feedback, and test across every model you plan to run the skill on.
📡 2026 intel
• The SKILL.md format is now an open standard: only name + description are required; spec-compliant runtimes
ignore any frontmatter keys they do not recognize, so skills stay portable across tools.
• Safety rule from the spec: avoid angle brackets (< or >) in frontmatter — they can inject unintended
instructions into the system prompt.
• The public anthropic/skills repo ships ready-made skills (document + example collections) you can install,
read, and copy as templates for your own.
Skills and their spec are in active development across model providers and agent tooling — expect folder conventions to keep shifting.
🔑 Key insight
Treat a skill like a small, well-tested program: a tight name + description so the agent triggers it, a lean body
that discloses detail progressively, the right degree of freedom for the task, and both a best-practice review
(skill-creator) and behavioral unit tests before it goes to production.
Next: bring these two skills into Jupyter notebooks and run them with the Claude Messages API using code-execution
tools, to produce outputs programmatically.
